title: Meta ships Muse Ember, a 10-cent-per-million-token agent workhorse
subtitle: Muse Ember targets the high-volume tier below Muse Wonder with a 1M-token context, multimodal input, and pricing that undercuts Claude Haiku 5.5 by roughly two-thirds.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta's Superintelligence Lab released Muse Ember on November 9, positioning it as the cheapest and lightest member of the Muse family. The published API ID is muse-ember-1.0, the context window is 1 million tokens, and the model accepts text, image, audio, and video as input. Pricing is about $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens — roughly a third of Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 per-task cost, on Meta's own benchmarks. Availability is immediate through the Meta Model API, Muse Code, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud. Weights are not being released, consistent with every prior Muse launch.

The framing is explicit: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume. Agent workloads burn through tokens on tool calls, routing, retrieval reranking, and bounded subtasks where a larger model is overkill, and the economics of running those workloads at frontier prices break on anything but low-traffic demos. Meta is betting that the market for cheap, high-context, multimodal inference is now large enough to justify a dedicated tier below its flagship, and that enterprises will route traffic between tiers through a planner — exactly the pattern Anthropic has been encouraging with Haiku and Opus, and that OpenAI has operationalized with GPT-6 and GPT-6.1 Sol. The 1M-token context is unusual at this price point: most sub-$1 models cap context well below that, which makes Ember attractive for ingest-heavy document workflows.

The caveats are the usual ones. Benchmarks published alongside a launch are self-reported — one third-party outlet noted Ember trails Claude Haiku on at least one coding benchmark — and comparisons on 'cost per task' depend heavily on how many retries and tool round-trips the model needs to complete the task. The strategic read is more interesting than the leaderboard: Meta is now shipping distinct product tiers on a cadence that resembles OpenAI and Anthropic, which is new for the company and signals that MSL has moved past the single-flagship-launch rhythm that defined the Muse Spark and Wonder releases.

A takeaway for learners: the race that matters for most applications is no longer the frontier benchmark. It is the cost curve at the bottom. A model priced at a tenth of a frontier tier, with usable quality on bounded tasks, changes what a product is willing to try — long-form document retrieval, aggressive tool use, per-user agents — because the economics shift from pilot to deploy. When evaluating a new model, calculate dollars-per-successful-task, not dollars-per-million-tokens: it is the number that actually determines whether a workflow is viable in production.
